CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation -> altered splicing and impaired ATM/TP53-mediated DNA repair -> formation of genomic fragile sites (and, occasionally, enhanced viral DNA integration) -> activation of oncogenic splice variants and downstream signaling -> increased metastasis/angiogenesis -> poor liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, upregulation of SF3B2 collaborates with key genomic custodians ATM and TP53 to both rewire RNA splicing and compromise DNA repair mechanisms. This dual perturbation leads to the generation of oncogenic splice variants and the formation of genomic fragile sites. These fragile regions, while primarily driving direct oncogenic signaling, may also serve as hotspots for sporadic viral DNA integration events, which further exacerbate genomic instability. The net effect is an enhanced activation of oncogenic pathways that promote metastasis and angiogenesis, resulting in a worsened prognosis. To test this, we will employ state-of-the-art RNA and DNA sequencing, CRISPR-mediated gene modulation, and proteomic interaction studies to clarify the molecular connections between splicing dysregulation, DNA repair impairment, and their impact on oncogenesis in liver cancers.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that the liver-specific splicing factor SF3B2, when upregulated in liver neoplasms, works together with pivotal genomic regulators ATM and TP53 to disrupt standard RNA splicing and DNA repair processes. This disruption leads not only to the generation of oncogenic splice variants but also to a compromised genomic surveillance system that may create ‘fragile’ genomic sites susceptible to viral DNA integration. Although direct markers of viral integration have been inconsistently observed, its sporadic occurrence can act as an additional accelerator of oncogenic signaling. Leveraging contemporary high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based gene editing, and proteomic interaction assays, we aim to delineate how SF3B2-driven alterations reprogram splicing networks, fortify genomic instability, and promote downstream activation of metastasis and angiogenesis. Our hypothesis bridges established roles of splicing dysregulation with a novel aspect of viral integration, thereby offering new molecular targets for therapeutic intervention in liver cancers.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on SF3B2 upregulation promoting viral DNA integration through the stabilization of splicing complexes and impaired DNA repair via ATM/TP53, leading to oncogenic signaling and poor prognosis. In the revised hypothesis, we have maintained these core elements—SF3B2 upregulation, modulation of splicing, interaction with ATM and TP53, and downstream activation of oncogenic pathways. However, in response to review feedback, we have clarified the mechanism by proposing that aberrant splicing not only creates oncogenic splice variants but also engenders genomic fragile sites which might predispose to viral integration, albeit as a secondary event. Additionally, we have enhanced practical implementability by incorporating advanced techniques (high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR, proteomics) to validate each step of the causal chain. This revision reinforces the causal chain: SF3B2 upregulation leads to dysregulated splicing and compromised DNA repair, resulting in genomic instability (fragile sites and occasional viral integration) that drives oncogenesis, metastasis, and angiogenesis.
